extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of mechanics, physics, and history/philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and critical commentary on foundational concepts and methodological principles in classical mechanics (mass, inertia, gravitation, frames of reference), mixing historical examples and philosophical analysis. Emphasizes how to define, measure, and justify core concepts and laws in mechanics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Isolation and superposition as analytic method
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of a phenomenon into mutually independent parts (isolation), and the composition of a phenomenon out of such parts (superposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Science should conceive phenomena as made up of sets of partial phenomena and at first study these partial phenomena in their purity; only when we know how each circumstance shares in the phenomenon as an entirety do we acquire command over the whole. (P. Volkmann quotation and author commentary.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Perspicuous deduction of mechanical results
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivations (e.g., expression for centrifugal force via Hamilton's hodograph) should be clear and perspicuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use transparent geometric/kinematic constructions (like hodographs) so that transformations of velocities and resulting accelerations are evident; approximate expansions must be justified by noting vanishing small terms (direction may change while magnitude remains).

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical hypotheses must avoid absurd consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed physical mechanism must not lead to absurd or observationally false implications (example: vortical ether implying lightest bodies receive greatest centripetal impulse).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine consequences of hypotheses (e.g., Huygens' critique of Descartes' vortical medium showing implausible mass-dependent centripetal impulses); rule out theories that require empirically impossible properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for mechanical/contact explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations in physics are preferable when rendered mechanically (via pressures and impacts/contact forces) rather than as unexplained action at a distance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historically, Huygens and others sought to replace action-at-a-distance by contact forces; later developments (Faraday, Maxwell) also emphasized contact/field-based conceptions that altered attitudes toward forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with empirical facts rather than speculative hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Start from well-established empirical facts (e.g., universal gravitation) and avoid ungrounded hypotheses where possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newton's stated reluctance to frame hypotheses is cited: deduce consequences from observed facts, and avoid speculative intermediary agencies unless needed to resolve contradictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational/experimental definition of mass
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantity 'mass' should be defined operationally (e.g., via the negative inverse ratio of mutually induced accelerations), determined by experiments such as impacts or Atwood-like machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mass-ratios are conventionally defined but must be shown by inquiry to be independent of the kinds and order of combination of bodies; experiments (centrifugal machines, impacts, electric/magnetic interactions) can determine mass-ratios practically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement conventions and inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of units/indicators (for temperature, time, etc.) is a convention, while the numerical values (ratios, laws) are results of empirical inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select arbitrarily chosen motions or indicators (angle of earth's rotation, path of a free body) that correspond closely to sensations but are robust against sensory disturbances; recognize conventions yet test invariance by experiment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat physical laws as empirically approximate and revisable
rubrics_metrics.description: Accept laws (e.g., law of inertia) as tolerably accurate approximations referenced to practical frames (fixed stars / Earth's rotation), subject to correction by future experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat foundational laws as metaphysical absolutes; refer them provisionally to observational frames and await empirical refinements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct application of inertia in theoretical arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the law of inertia properly when constructing or evaluating explanatory theories (e.g., Galileo's tide theory fails from an incorrect/incomplete use of inertia).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether assumed relative motions and boundary conditions truly produce the claimed effects; avoid negative or mistaken conceptions of inertia that yield illusory conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational definition of motion and rotation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer relational accounts of motion: only relative motions exist and labels like 'absolute rotation' should be understood as relative rotation with respect to some chosen reference (commonly the fixed stars).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centrifugal forces arise relative to certain bodies (e.g., fixed stars); experiments imagined to swap rotation between system and stars are meaningless in sense-perception—avoid metaphysical absolutism and state clearly the reference used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of particular determination for inertial frames
rubrics_metrics.description: One may define an inertial coordinate system by fixing the rigid (preserved) relations of three noncollinear material points such that other free points move in straight lines relative to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is largely a convention for coordinates; the empirical content lies in whether additional free points also move inertially with respect to that system—thus one must check by inquiry, not merely by definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid treating small isolated subsystems as wholly adequate
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyses that consider only a minimal number of isolated points and exclude the rest of the world are inadmissible for fully grounding concepts like inertia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Global considerations (e.g., the fixed stars) historically provided foundations for the law of inertia; neglecting the rest of the universe may omit essential influences and make statements merely conventional rather than empirically grounded.
